opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I've updated on this a fair amount. I used to be fairly skeptical. A lot of those models start from a production function with some elasticity of substitution between compute and labor and some returns-to-research parameter, then turn the crank. My reaction was always: the conclusions are basically baked into the assumptions, and we don't have good estimates for the parameters that matter most. So what are we learning?

I still think that critique has some force. But I've come to appreciate what these models are good for. They're less about prediction and more about making your assumptions explicit. If someone says "AI will automate AI research and we'll get an intelligence explosion," a simple model forces you to ask: explosion under what conditions? Does it depend on whether compute is a hard bottleneck? On whether ideas get harder to find faster than effective researcher count grows? Seeing which parameters the qualitative outcome is sensitive to is genuinely useful, because it tells you what to go measure.

That's connected to my own work. Much of the empirical side, like measuring how long a task models can complete, or how much they speed up actual researchers, feeds directly into those parameters. Before, the models felt untethered. Now there's more data to plug in, and the models tell you which measurements would change your mind. It's a nice division of labor: theorists say "this number matters a lot," and empiricists go figure out roughly what it is.

The caveat is that I'm wary of people over-reading the outputs. If a model says takeoff happens in some range of years, that's conditional on a lot of structure that could be wrong. Things like how messy real research is, or how much tacit knowledge and hard-to-measure judgment matters, tend to get abstracted away, and I suspect that's where much of the real-world friction lives. So I'd say I'm more positive than I was, but mainly as a tool for clarifying disagreements rather than as a forecasting machine.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses economic models as tools for making assumptions explicit and identifying useful measurements, but does not suggest that AI progress has deeper systematicity beneath apparent contingency or arbitrariness.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think my view on this has shifted a fair amount. A few years ago I was pretty skeptical of them. My instinct was that the stylized models people were writing down, you know, production functions with AI as a substitute for labor, or these simple growth models with a feedback loop between AI and research, were just too abstracted away from the actual mechanics of how progress happens to tell you anything useful. I was coming at this from the empirical side, building benchmarks, looking at how systems actually behave on specific tasks, and that work made the abstractions feel almost unserious. Like, you can't fit a Cobb-Douglas production function to what GPQA is measuring.

I think I've come around to a more moderate position. The thing I underrated is that these models aren't really trying to be predictive in a precise sense. What they're good at is forcing you to be explicit about your assumptions. If you believe AI is going to dramatically accelerate AI research, there's a question lurking underneath that: what's the elasticity of substitution between compute and human researcher labor? Does the bottleneck move? Are there complementary inputs, like experiments or real-world feedback loops, that don't scale when you add more cognitive labor? And when you actually try to write that down, you discover that a lot of the disagreements people have are really disagreements about one or two parameters they've never named.

So I now think of the models as a kind of disciplined way of having the argument, rather than a forecasting tool. The failure mode is when people take the output of the model as the conclusion rather than as a translation of their inputs. If you put in strong substitutability and a research feedback loop, you get an explosion. That's not a finding, that's what you assumed.

The other thing I'd say is that the empirical work and the modeling work need each other more than I used to think. The models tell you what you'd need to measure to actually settle a question, and the benchmarks and evaluations are where you go try to measure it. Things like how long a task an AI system can do autonomously, or how much of a researcher's week is actually automatable, those are exactly the quantities a reasonable model points you toward. So I've gone from seeing them as a distraction to seeing them as a pretty useful scaffolding, as long as you're honest about how much of the conclusion is baked into the setup.

r001.rationale: The response discusses abstract models as a way to clarify assumptions and guide measurement, but it does not suggest that AI progress has deeper systematicity despite appearing contingent or arbitrary up close.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re useful for clarifying assumptions, but I’m more cautious about treating them as forecasts. A model can help you ask, “If AI makes this kind of work much cheaper, what becomes the bottleneck?” That’s a useful question, even if the model doesn’t tell you when that happens or how large the effect will be.

The hard part is connecting the abstractions to what AI systems can actually do. Automating some tasks doesn’t necessarily mean you can automate a whole research process, and that distinction can matter a lot for the conclusions. So I’d want to look at which results survive different assumptions about those details. I put more weight on a model that helps identify what we need to measure than on a precise trajectory that comes out of it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses models’ usefulness, assumptions, and task automation, but it does not suggest that AI progress has deeper systematicity beneath an apparently contingent or arbitrary surface.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re useful for clarifying what assumptions are doing the work, but I’m less confident in them as a way of predicting how AI progress will unfold. You can write down a model where AI automates research, which produces better AI, which accelerates research again. That helps you see why a feedback loop could matter. But it doesn’t tell you how strong that feedback loop is, or which bottlenecks become important along the way.

So I’d want to connect the model to concrete questions: what tasks can these systems actually do, how reliably can they do them, and how much does improving those tasks speed up the overall research process? The abstract model gives you a framework for asking those questions. A lot of the predictive value comes from getting the empirical answers right.

r001.rationale: The response discusses a possible AI research feedback loop and the limits of abstract models, but it does not suggest that AI progress has deeper systematicity despite seeming contingent and arbitrary up close.
